newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cancer experts to tackle mammogram confusion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cancer experts to tackle mammogram confusion.

text.p: Breast cancer experts will seek this week to put to rest a long-running and emotional controversy about whether women in their 40s need regular mammograms.

For several years, medical groups and women's advocacy organisations have put out different recommendations, leaving women and their doctors uncertain about when they should have the breast cancer screening X-ray.

Hoping to clear up the confusion, the National Institutes of Health is convening a three-day conference to see if the independent experts can reach a consensus on screening for women in their 40s and put women's minds at rest.
"There's a lot of fear out there for women in their 40s," said Michelle Melin, director of patient services at the Y-Me women's health advocacy group.

The National Cancer Institute recommends mammograms every one or two years for women age 50 to 69. But in 1993, reversing its own previous advice, it did not recommend mammograms for most women in their 40s.
But the American Cancer Society and some major medical groups recommend mammograms for women in their 40s every year or two. After 50, the cancer society recommends annual checks.
Nor is there unanimity among women's health and breast cancer advocacy groups.
"There is no universal agreement on screening younger women, including who should be screened and at what interval," said National Cancer Institute director Dr. Richard Klausner.
About 20 to 25 percent of the 185,000 new cases of breast cancer that will be diagnosed in the United States this year will be in women under 50.

Experts agree that mammograms for women in their 50s and 60s can save lives. Many studies have shown that regular mammograms could lower by about one-third the breast cancer death rate in that age group, but the evidence for women in their 40s has been unclear.

"So far mammography for younger women hasn't been shown to save lives," Cynthia Pearson, director of the National Women's Health Network, said. That group recommends mammograms for women in their 40s only if they have gone through menopause.

There are various theories about why the data so far have not shown a clear benefit to women under 50, ranging from the possibility that the studies have been too small to detect a significant advantage to the theory that many cancers that strike younger women are aggressive and hard to treat so that even mammogram detection does not always improve the odds.

The independent experts on the NIH panel will review 32 new studies from around the world. Although the hope is for clarity, there is no guarantee that the new data will be sufficient to enable the panel to reach a clear-cut agreement. More research could be needed in the coming years.
Neither panel head Dr. Leon Gordis of Johns Hopkins public health school nor the other members are permitted to talk about such consensus conferences in advance.

Mammography is far from an ideal technology. About 80 percent of the suspicious lesions spotted turn out to be harmless, but women still have to undergo invasive biopsies and huge stress to determine they are not cancerous.

Nor does a mammography pick up all small cancers, particularly in younger women with denser breast tissue. And it cannot evaluate risk or determine which woman who walks out with a "clean" mammogram could start developing cancerous cells soon after.

Many researchers are working on alternative screening techniques, including some digital imagery borrowing from the military and intelligence communities, that may in coming years provide women with better screening tools.
Genetic research, as well as development of tests that can pick up molecular markers that identify cancer risk, may also revolutionise screening in the next decade or so.

Breast cancer is one of the most dreaded diseases for women, who have a one-in-eight chance of developing the disease sometime in their lifetime. About 44,500 U.S. women die from breast cancer each year.
